overview: This record represents independent Chad from 1960, following French colonial rule. Its borders enclose many communities with distinct histories; the modern republic is not interchangeable with earlier Kanem, Wadai or other states.

periods.title: Independence and conflict
periods.summary: Chad became independent in 1960; fighting in N’Djamena forced a diplomatic evacuation in 1980.

periods.title: Habré’s rule
periods.summary: Hissène Habré’s government was later the subject of an international criminal trial.

periods.title: Déby’s long presidency
periods.summary: Idriss Déby’s rule ended with his death in 2021.

periods.title: Political transition
periods.summary: A military council followed Déby’s death; a new constitution was adopted in 2023.

items.text: Chad’s independence was proclaimed on 11 August 1960. Diplomatic records also preserve an older capital name: the American embassy opened at Fort Lamy in 1961, in the city now called N’Djamena. Names on old letters can reveal political changes that a modern map conceals.

Hissène Habré ruled from 1982 to 1990. In 2016, the Extraordinary African Chambers in Senegal convicted him of torture, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Survivors’ efforts to secure a trial are part of Chad’s history alongside the rulers whose actions they challenged.

A small writing sample comes from the 2020 children’s comic title “Lafya,” which UNICEF translates from Ngambaye as “peace.” Its eight-year-old heroine learns about life during school closures. Versions in French, Arabic and Ngambaye show that public education can use several languages within one country.

sections.title: Modern discoveries of a much older past

items.text: The Franco-Chadian research mission found a nearly complete skull, jaw material and teeth at Toros-Menalla site TM 266. Scientists assigned them to Sahelanthropus tchadensis, around seven million years old. Published work identifies them as evidence relevant to early human evolution, not the remains of a Chadian nation millions of years ago.

Other fossils make the setting more surprising than today’s desert suggests. Fish, crocodiles and water-associated mammals occur alongside animals linked to woodland and savannah. In 2002, researchers used these remains and sediments to reconstruct a lakeside environment near sandy desert. Ancient landscapes can hide inside modern dry ground.

Around Lake Chad, dihé is a food harvested from blue-green microorganisms in shallow waters. FAO’s account describes women straining it through palm baskets, letting water drain in sand basins, cutting the thickened material into pieces and drying them in the sun. Harvesting and processing require learned skill.

In field notes from March 2002 near Boudou Andja, women’s leader Harita Cierom asked for sturdy clothing, gloves, boots and support for a producers’ association. Salty water made the work hard on skin and clothes. Her request puts the workers, rather than only the finished food, into the historical record.

Massa communities live on both sides of the Logone River in Chad and Cameroon. In the annual Guruna retreat, boys and men take cattle to a camp away from home. Elders teach cattle care alongside community history, music, dance, handicrafts and wrestling: school can happen far from a classroom.

UNESCO’s Guruna account describes girls helping prepare food and decorations without staying overnight. Older women transmit those skills, while fathers, elders and specialist masters guide other instruction. Public ceremonies and performances let participants demonstrate what they have learned; the learning involves the wider community.

Between 2000 and 2005, researchers and health teams tested combined visits for nomadic families and their livestock. Physicians and veterinarians shared transport and equipment while providing their separate vaccinations. Bringing both services together reduced costs and reached more women and children per day than human-only rounds in the study.

A later study in Danamadji found that pastoralists valued combined vaccination, but keeping the programme running required dependable funding and coordination. Even livestock enclosures mattered for safe, workable vaccination days. The useful invention here was organizing services around mobile families rather than expecting families to fit a distant clinic.

During the pandemic, Chad used radio, television and phones for lessons. UNICEF’s May 2021 case study also reported handwashing kits, soap and bleach delivered to at least 1,083 primary schools. Reopening involved water and hygiene as well as books; a classroom timetable alone could not do the job.

ending.text: Chad continued after Idriss Déby’s death in 2021 and the military takeover led by his son. The 2023 constitution again described a sovereign republic. These institutional changes do not mark an ending for Chad’s many peoples or their cross-border connections.
